According to a comprehensive scientific review published in npj Sustainable Agriculture by an international research team led by Daoyuan Jin, agentic artificial intelligence represents an evolving technological paradigm designed to tackle operational hurdles in global crop production. Unlike earlier agricultural software relying on rigid dashboards or isolated machine learning models, agentic systems deploy autonomous entities that receive high-level objectives rather than granular instructions. These systems iteratively gather environmental data, query external tools, generate structured plans, and execute multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention. While artificial intelligence has begun entering agriculture through specialized chatbots and diagnostic models, the review emphasizes that agentic workflows expand these capabilities by coupling reasoning-capable foundation models with structured planning, active environment interaction, and modular tool use across phenomics, crop management, field robotics, and policy. The review traces the technical taxonomy underpinning these systems, delineating the progression from basic autonomous entities to intelligent agents and coordinated multi-agent architectures. In artificial intelligence research, an intelligent agent is formally characterized by three operational hallmarks: reactivity to environmental dynamics, proactivity in pursuing designated objectives, and social capability to communicate and cooperate with other autonomous entities or human managers. While early agent research in the 1990s and 2000s relied on rigid multi-layer frameworks such as Touring Machines and InteRRaP, the integration of large language models provides unprecedented flexibility, contextual comprehension, and dynamic problem-solving capacity. Modern architectures combine these foundation models with retrieval-augmented generation and external memory modules. Retrieval-augmented generation enables models to ground reasoning in external agronomic databases rather than remaining confined to static pre-training weights, while external memory retains critical seasonal context beyond the restrictive boundaries of standard model context windows, facilitating sustained adaptation across changing farm conditions. At their architectural core, agricultural intelligent agents operate within a continuous four-part feedback loop comprising perception, reasoning and decision-making, action, and continuous learning and adaptation. Perception captures ambient conditions through diverse sensory channels, including visual, thermal, olfactory, haptic, and acoustic sensors tailored to specific biological and field tasks. AI agent tools are arriving fast, but the controls to run them safely are not keeping pace. The brief reviews three latest releases in 2026: 1. OpenAI put its Agents API into public beta, giving developers a managed Codex harness for building and running cloud agents. 2. Salesforce announced new Agentforce agents for sales, service, commerce, and workforce tasks. 3. Google made Agent Development Kit for Kotlin 1.0 generally available, matching ADK 1.0 Core with multi-agent teamwork and resumable sessions. Gravitee surveyed 750 senior tech leaders in April. Agent numbers had about doubled in four months, yet monitoring covered only about 52%. Just 9.5% of companies said they secured more than 81% of their agents. VentureBeat Pulse Research surveyed 107 companies in June. 54% had a confirmed agent security incident or a near miss. Only 32% gave each agent its own scoped, managed identity. Exabeam and Sapio Research surveyed 600 security and finance leaders. 48% named agents with too much, stolen, or unplanned access as their top threat. Only 28% pointed to outside attackers. The brief says the gap comes from how the tools are built and sold, not from careless teams. Most vendors find it difficult to grasp your permission rules or which systems an agent must never touch. Tech experts recommend that each company must decide what AI agents can run alone, what they can reach, and which actions need approval. Agents inside customer portals and dashboards raise the same questions, so firms offering [web application development services](https://uniquesoftwaredev.com/services/web-applications/) must plan for them early. The brief names four areas that usually need extra work: * A separate, limited identity for each agent, not a shared account * Audit logs detailed enough to show what an agent did * Approval steps at set points in a workflow * Links between agents and existing business systems Healthcare, finance, transportation, and government teams must also meet federal, state, and industry rules on access, data handling, and audit trails. A shipping company adding an agent to dispatch or fleet data must fit current systems, which is taken care of by a [logistics software development company](https://uniquesoftwaredev.com/industries/custom-transportation-software-development/). Shared accounts cause special trouble, since nobody can tell which agent did what. The brief also suggests a small proof of concept, because problems cost far less to fix early. The brief is available on request. highlights.content: [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/growyourstartup.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/front-sociable-1.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [Business](https://sociable.co/business/) # How training approaches have shaped the evolution of large language models November 6, 2026 [![](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/getty-images-Nu7LYcNFH-4-unsplash.jpg)](https://sociable.co/business/how-training-approaches-have-shaped-the-evolution-of-large-language-models/) ## Act 1: Predict the next token (2018 to 2020) **GPT-1 (2018): the objective works.** [GPT-1](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) was a 117M-parameter transformer trained on one task: predict the next token in about 7,000 books. To do that well, it had to pick up grammar, facts, and meaning on its own. Fine-tuned on small labeled datasets, it beat purpose-built models on 9 of 12 benchmarks. Next-token prediction turned out to be a way to learn language itself. **GPT-2 (2019): scale, and tasks start to appear.** [GPT-2](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) grew to 1.5B parameters trained on 40 GB of web text. Without fine-tuning, it began to summarize, translate, and answer questions **zero-shot**. The results were rough, but they hinted that scale alone unlocks new abilities. **GPT-3 (2020): no more fine-tuning.** At 175B parameters, [GPT-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165?ref=hackernoon.com) could learn a task from a description and a few examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Using a language model no longer required a labeled dataset, just a good prompt. [Scaling laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361?ref=hackernoon.com) showed that bigger models would keep improving predictably. ### The catch Next-token prediction teaches a model what text *looks like*, not how it *should* respond. A pretrained model: * **continues instead of answering.** Ask “How do I bake bread?” and it may write five more questions, because that’s what often follows a question online. * **doesn’t know when to stay quiet.** If it knows how to do something dangerous, nothing in its objective tells it not to say so. * **mirrors the internet**, made-up facts and toxic text included. The capability was there. It just wasn’t pointed anywhere useful. ## Act 2: Be a helpful assistant (2022) The fix was a second training phase: **post-training**. OpenAI’s [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155?ref=hackernoon.com) recipe had three steps: 1. Humans write good example answers, and the model learns to imitate them. 2. Humans rank the model’s answers, and a reward model learns their preferences. 3. The LLM is optimized against that reward model with **reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)**. The effect was dramatic. Raters preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT over the 175B GPT-3. The right objective beat 100x more parameters. In November 2022, OpenAI applied this recipe to a GPT-3.5 model tuned for dialogue and released [ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/?ref=hackernoon.com). It answered instead of rambling and declined some harmful requests, and it reached an estimated 100 million users in about two months. From here on, the big advances happened *after* pretraining. ## Act 3: Think before you answer (2021 to 2025) **Math and code came first.** From 2021 to 2024, labs pushed hard on both, from [Codex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374?ref=hackernoon.com) to [trained math verifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168?ref=hackernoon.com) to [step-by-step math verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050?ref=hackernoon.com). highlights.content: [![Homeland411](https://homeland411.com/wp-content/themes/homeland411/images/homeland411-logo-modern.webp)](https://homeland411.com/) ![Homeland411](https://homeland411.com/wp-content/themes/homeland411/images/homeland411-logo-modern.webp) # AI Agent Security Risks: Kaspersky Warns Against Trusting LLMs by Default ![Advanced systems engineering laboratory bench with microkernel hardware testing modules and diagnostic displays](https://homeland411.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/hero_kaspersky_cyber_immunity_ai_agent_watermarked.webp) Enterprise cybersecurity architecture must treat large language models inside autonomous artificial intelligence agents as untrusted software components by default. A comprehensive research paper released by Kaspersky demonstrates that probabilistic neural networks cannot reliably distinguish system instructions from unverified data inputs. Security researchers argue that deploying external bolt-on defensive filters fails to mitigate indirect prompt injection or unauthorized tool execution. The investigation outlines an architectural paradigm shift based on Cyber Immunity principles. This methodology enforces hardware-level isolation, deterministic policy monitors, and microkernel sandboxes around non-deterministic reasoning cores. Security specialists published their technical framework in an official [Kaspersky Cyber Immunity research report](https://lp.kaspersky.com/global/ai-agent-cyber-immunity/). Building native resilience directly into the operational fabric prevents compromised agents from hijacking enterprise networks. Modern autonomous agents execute multi-step planning loops, query internal document stores, and invoke arbitrary application programming interfaces across corporate perimeters. When an agent reads unauthenticated emails or parses untrusted web content, embedded adversarial commands can overwrite developer instructions. These instruction poisoning vectors mirror software vulnerabilities exposed in Homeland411’s reporting on [malicious prompt injection and instruction poisoning](https://homeland411.com/hackers-hide-malicious-instructions-ai-coding-projects-hijack-assistants/) in developer ecosystems. Without hardware-enforced compartmentalization, a subverted foundation model inherits all administrative rights allocated to the host application process. **Never Miss An Update**Follow us on Google News to get our latest security, defense and cyber reporting in your feed. It’s free and takes one tap. The research emphasizes that traditional software development paradigms assume core application code executes deterministically according to strict mathematical logic. Foundation models operate probabilistically. This fundamental reality renders neural weights incapable of acting as their own security reference monitors. Treating the language model as a trusted compute component exposes organizations to catastrophic lateral movement and credential exfiltration. These architectural vulnerabilities parallel real-world intrusions documented in Homeland411’s ongoing analysis of [autonomous agentic exploitation of cloud secrets](https://homeland411.com/microsoft-warns-agentic-ai-weaponized-cloud-secrets/) across corporate infrastructure. Kaspersky proposes applying microkernel isolation models that strictly segregate the model reasoning core from execution tools and data pipelines. By stripping the probabilistic model of direct operating system privileges, security architects eliminate single points of failure across automated workflows. A dedicated, deterministic security monitor intercepts every outbound function call. The monitor enforces immutable access control rules before any network packet transmits. This rigorous design pattern restricts the trusted computing base to mathematically verifiable components that resist adversarial manipulation. ## Traditional Agent Perimeters Versus Cyber Immune System Architecture The architectural divergence between conventional perimeter wrappers ...

highlights.content: ![EurekAlert! Science News](/images/logo-2x.png) ![A service of the American Association for the Advancement of Science](/images/brand.png) ![EurekAlert! Science News](/images/logo-2x.png) ![A service of the American Association for the Advancement of Science](/images/brand.png) # Can LLMs help judge how intelligently autonomous vehicles behave in traffic? Tsinghua University Press ![Overview of the Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework for high-level autonomous vehicle intelligence.](https://mediasvc.eurekalert.org/Api/v1/Multimedia/9b700144-7158-4e5d-be1c-9fb7e06129d2/Rendition/low-res/Content/Public) **image: The framework converts autonomous-vehicle interaction data into structured language for LLM-based, expert-like assessment, then maps five-dimensional objective metrics to intelligence scores through an attention-based neural network. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic.** [view more](/multimedia/1161024) The framework converts autonomous-vehicle interaction data into structured language for LLM-based, expert-like assessment, then maps five-dimensional objective metrics to intelligence scores through an attention-based neural network. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. Credit: Communications in Transportation Research Self-driving vehicles are moving from pilot projects toward wider commercial deployment, but a vehicle that performs well on conventional tests may still behave in ways that feel hesitant, abrupt or disruptive in real traffic. Researchers at Tongji University have developed a new framework designed to evaluate the overall “intelligence” of high-level autonomous driving systems, rather than judging isolated functions such as braking or lane keeping alone. The study, “Towards the Intelligence Evaluation of High-level Autonomous Vehicles: A Subjective-Objective Mapping Method via LLM,” introduces a Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework. It combines measurable driving data with expert-style assessments generated by a large language model (LLM), then trains an attention-based neural network to learn how objective indicators relate to the broader judgments that human experts make when observing vehicle behavior. The team published their study in [*Communications in Transportation Research*](https://www.sciopen.com/journal/2097-5023) (<https://doi.org/10.26599/COMMTR.2026.9640041>). “A high-level autonomous vehicle should not be evaluated only by whether it avoids a crash,” says Peng Hang, corresponding author of the study and a research professor at Tongji University. “Its behavior should also be judged by whether it moves smoothly, completes tasks efficiently, interacts reasonably with other road users and avoids unnecessarily disrupting surrounding traffic.” **From raw trajectories to expert-like evaluation** The framework evaluates five complementary aspects of autonomous driving behavior: safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. It uses interaction segments from the Waymo Open Dataset, including following, merging and crossing situations. Unlike earlier agricultural software relying on rigid dashboards or isolated machine learning models, agentic systems deploy autonomous entities that receive high-level objectives rather than granular instructions. These systems iteratively gather environmental data, query external tools, generate structured plans, and execute multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention. While artificial intelligence has begun entering agriculture through specialized chatbots and diagnostic models, the review emphasizes that agentic workflows expand these capabilities by coupling reasoning-capable foundation models with structured planning, active environment interaction, and modular tool use across phenomics, crop management, field robotics, and policy. Security researchers argue that deploying external bolt-on defensive filters fails to mitigate indirect prompt injection or unauthorized tool execution. The investigation outlines an architectural paradigm shift based on Cyber Immunity principles. This methodology enforces hardware-level isolation, deterministic policy monitors, and microkernel sandboxes around non-deterministic reasoning cores. Security specialists published their technical framework in an official [Kaspersky Cyber Immunity research report](https://lp.kaspersky.com/global/ai-agent-cyber-immunity/). LLMs.titleZh: How training approaches have shaped the evolution of large language models
LLMs.content: [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/growyourstartup.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/front-sociable-1.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [Business](https://sociable.co/business/) # How training approaches have shaped the evolution of large language models November 6, 2026 [![](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/getty-images-Nu7LYcNFH-4-unsplash.jpg)](https://sociable.co/business/how-training-approaches-have-shaped-the-evolution-of-large-language-models/) ## Act 1: Predict the next token (2018 to 2020) **GPT-1 (2018): the objective works.** [GPT-1](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) was a 117M-parameter transformer trained on one task: predict the next token in about 7,000 books. To do that well, it had to pick up grammar, facts, and meaning on its own. Fine-tuned on small labeled datasets, it beat purpose-built models on 9 of 12 benchmarks. Next-token prediction turned out to be a way to learn language itself. **GPT-2 (2019): scale, and tasks start to appear.** [GPT-2](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) grew to 1.5B parameters trained on 40 GB of web text. Without fine-tuning, it began to summarize, translate, and answer questions **zero-shot**. The results were rough, but they hinted that scale alone unlocks new abilities. **GPT-3 (2020): no more fine-tuning.** At 175B parameters, [GPT-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165?ref=hackernoon.com) could learn a task from a description and a few examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Using a language model no longer required a labeled dataset, just a good prompt. [Scaling laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361?ref=hackernoon.com) showed that bigger models would keep improving predictably. ### The catch Next-token prediction teaches a model what text *looks like*, not how it *should* respond. A pretrained model: * **continues instead of answering.** Ask “How do I bake bread?” and it may write five more questions, because that’s what often follows a question online. * **doesn’t know when to stay quiet.** If it knows how to do something dangerous, nothing in its objective tells it not to say so. * **mirrors the internet**, made-up facts and toxic text included. The capability was there. It just wasn’t pointed anywhere useful. ## Act 2: Be a helpful assistant (2022) The fix was a second training phase: **post-training**. OpenAI’s [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155?ref=hackernoon.com) recipe had three steps: 1. Humans write good example answers, and the model learns to imitate them. 2. Humans rank the model’s answers, and a reward model learns their preferences. 3. The LLM is optimized against that reward model with **reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)**. The effect was dramatic. Raters preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT over the 175B GPT-3. The right objective beat 100x more parameters. In November 2022, OpenAI applied this recipe to a GPT-3.5 model tuned for dialogue and released [ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/?ref=hackernoon.com). It answered instead of rambling and declined some harmful requests, and it reached an estimated 100 million users in about two months. From here on, the big advances happened *after* pretraining. ## Act 3: Think before you answer (2021 to 2025) **Math and code came first.** From 2021 to 2024, labs pushed hard on both, from [Codex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374?ref=hackernoon.com) to [trained math verifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168?ref=hackernoon.com) to [step-by-step math verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050?ref=hackernoon.com). The two domains share one useful property: the answer can be checked automatically. A math answer matches, or it doesn’t; code passes its tests, or it doe...

Tsinghua University Press ![Overview of the Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework for high-level autonomous vehicle intelligence.](https://mediasvc.eurekalert.org/Api/v1/Multimedia/9b700144-7158-4e5d-be1c-9fb7e06129d2/Rendition/low-res/Content/Public) **image: The framework converts autonomous-vehicle interaction data into structured language for LLM-based, expert-like assessment, then maps five-dimensional objective metrics to intelligence scores through an attention-based neural network. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic.** [view more](/multimedia/1161024) The framework converts autonomous-vehicle interaction data into structured language for LLM-based, expert-like assessment, then maps five-dimensional objective metrics to intelligence scores through an attention-based neural network. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. Credit: Communications in Transportation Research Self-driving vehicles are moving from pilot projects toward wider commercial deployment, but a vehicle that performs well on conventional tests may still behave in ways that feel hesitant, abrupt or disruptive in real traffic. Researchers at Tongji University have developed a new framework designed to evaluate the overall “intelligence” of high-level autonomous driving systems, rather than judging isolated functions such as braking or lane keeping alone. The study, “Towards the Intelligence Evaluation of High-level Autonomous Vehicles: A Subjective-Objective Mapping Method via LLM,” introduces a Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework. It combines measurable driving data with expert-style assessments generated by a large language model (LLM), then trains an attention-based neural network to learn how objective indicators relate to the broader judgments that human experts make when observing vehicle behavior. The team published their study in [*Communications in Transportation Research*](https://www.sciopen.com/journal/2097-5023) (<https://doi.org/10.26599/COMMTR.2026.9640041>). “A high-level autonomous vehicle should not be evaluated only by whether it avoids a crash,” says Peng Hang, corresponding author of the study and a research professor at Tongji University. “Its behavior should also be judged by whether it moves smoothly, completes tasks efficiently, interacts reasonably with other road users and avoids unnecessarily disrupting surrounding traffic.” **From raw trajectories to expert-like evaluation** The framework evaluates five complementary aspects of autonomous driving behavior: safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. It uses interaction segments from the Waymo Open Dataset, including following, merging and crossing situations. To improve coverage of rare but important poor-performance cases, the researchers also augmented the dataset with physically feasible low-score interaction samples. In total, the study constructed 5,200 valid interaction segments for training and evaluation. Because language models are not naturally suited to interpreting raw vehicle trajectories and map data, the researchers developed a Data-Language Mapping Module. This component converts key interaction events, vehicle states and abnormal motions into structured natural-language descriptions. The descriptions are combined with autonomous-driving knowledge, traffic rules and driving-behavior guidance, enabling the LLM to assess the interaction in an expert-like manner. LLMs.titleZh: Researchers develop AI tool to improve crisis communication  – Texas A&M Stories
LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [Texas A&M Stories](https://stories.tamu.edu) [View All Stories](/stories/) Share this [Science & Tech](https://stories.tamu.edu/category/science-technology/) # Researchers develop AI tool to improve crisis communication The system filters and categorizes disaster, weather and humanitarian reports to help emergency professionals quickly find relevant information during emergency response. Nov. 6, 2026 By Gabby Shultz, Texas A&M University Division of Marketing and Communications 2 min. read ![A photo of emergency responders in a command center with computer monitors on all of the walls.](https://stories.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20241217_Emergency_Operations_Center_Ribbon_Cutting_CS-10-e1793713629856-1408x793.jpg) Texas A&M researchers are developing an AI-based tool to help emergency managers quickly sort through the flood of information that emerges during crises such as hurricanes. Credit: Courtney Sacco/Texas A&M AgriLife During a disaster, emergency managers need quick, reliable data to make decisions, but the vast and changing stream of information that emerges during a crisis can make it difficult to distinguish facts from noise. Researchers from Texas A&M University are working to change that through the development of a tool that uses artificial intelligence to sort through the confusion. Led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Bo Li, Dr. Ali Mostafavi and Kai Yin in the [Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering](https://engineering.tamu.edu/civil/index.html), the work uses a large language model to filter the information that emerges during crises such as hurricanes, when emergency officials must make quick decisions while monitoring weather conditions, damage reports, public requests for assistance, search-and-rescue needs and more. In a [recent study on crisis-related social media classification](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1474034626005288), researchers used a benchmark of human-annotated social media posts from multiple disaster events. The model was designed to categorize crisis-related information into three areas: disaster-related, weather-related, and humanitarian information. The model goes even further into classifying each post by event type, informativeness, and humanitarian information type. Li said organizing information in categories could allow emergency personnel to more easily locate details relevant to their needs, such as updates on storm conditions, reports of damage or requests for aid and rescue. The system is under development and has not been deployed during an active disaster. “The team plans to build an AI agent that emergency professionals can talk to when disaster strikes,” Li said. “Ultimately, we want to move from classification toward a more interactive AI system that can better support situational awareness during disasters.” As disasters become more frequent and the amount of available information continues to grow, the researchers say AI-based tools could help response agencies reduce the time spent sorting reports and focus more quickly on decisions that support affected communities. LLMs.title: AI Backtest Guardrail Fails: Benchmark Finds Date Prompt Cuts GPT-5 Knowledge Claims 39% to 1%
LLMs.titleZh: AI Backtest Guardrail Fails: Benchmark Finds Date Prompt Cuts GPT-5 Knowledge Claims 39% to 1%
LLMs.content: Telling GPT-5 to answer as of a past date cuts the share of answers claiming prior knowledge from 39% to 1%, while its accuracy moves only from 76% to 75%, according to FinDendro, a benchmark that a 15-author team posted to arXiv on Nov. 4. That means a standard backtesting safeguard hides what an AI model knows without removing it, so the authors conclude that a financial backtest inside a model's training window cannot be certified leak-free by asking the model, instructing it, or trusting its vendor's stated cutoff. GPT-5 answers 76% of FinDendro's controlled facts correctly but claims to know only 38% of them, and it still gets 61% right among the facts it says it does not know, the authors report. Dividing 76% by 38% gives a 2-to-1 gap between what GPT-5 gets right and what it claims to know, a ratio computed here from the paper's figures rather than one the authors state. Practitioners rely on three safeguards against leakage: evaluating only after the vendor-stated cutoff, instructing the model to answer as of the forecast date, and asking the model for its own cutoff. FinDendro tests all three against 2,226 dated U.S. facts and finds that none reliably separates what a model learned from what it can genuinely predict. ### Date Prompt Cuts GPT-5 Knowledge Claims to 1% While Accuracy Holds at 75% In FinDendro's dated-prediction task, a prefix asks the model to answer as of a past date. For GPT-5, that prefix cut the share of answers claiming prior knowledge from 0.39 to 0.01, while accuracy moved from 0.76 to 0.75. The model changes what it says about its own knowledge; what it answers correctly stays almost the same. A separate preprint, "Simulated Ignorance Fails," reached a similar verdict on forecasting questions. Across 477 competition-level questions and nine models, cutoff instructions left a 52% performance gap between simulated ignorance and true ignorance. Step-by-step reasoning did not suppress prior knowledge, and reasoning-optimized models showed worse fidelity despite better reasoning traces, the authors report. ### How Does FinDendro Test What a Model Knows? FinDendro's name echoes dendrochronology, the method that dates tree rings to the exact year they formed by matching ring patterns against samples of known age. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Riemann 13.1B Model: NLL Falls 1.323 to 1.310 [2026] ![Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp) [Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/) Updated Nov 6, 2026 · 15 min read Riemann Computing Inc. published a technical account on October 28, 2026 that explains how it grew a 163-million-parameter checkpoint into *My Name is Riemann*, a decoder-only language model with 13.1 billion parameters. The account came through the OpenPeer AI organization on Hugging Face, and the [model card for the prerelease](https://huggingface.co/OpenPeerAI/My-Name-is-Riemann-Prerelease/blame/4b08de9a557e2b55a6b21ebb1f3bb2e160a34144/README.md) lists the exact count at 13,110,702,080 parameters. The Riemann Computing technical account matters less for the headline size than for the method. The team did not train a 13.1B network from random weights. It started from the published weights of OpenPeerAI/OpenPeerLLM, then climbed a six-rung growth ladder with a custom tool called OpenPeer-AI-NTK-Trainer. The account also discloses hardware, an evaluation set and a before-and-after result for a stage-six controller. We covered the October prerelease and its spec sheet in our earlier piece on [Riemann’s 13.1B-parameter model reaching Hugging Face](https://shattered.io/riemann-computing-13b-ai-model-prerelease-demo-2026/). This analysis skips that ground and asks a narrower question: what does the new technical account prove, what does it leave open, and what should developers and buyers of open weights do with it today. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Riemann Computing Published on October 28 The technical account is a write-up of the development process, released by the OpenPeer AI organization on Hugging Face. Riemann Computing also pushed the story through press channels. A PRWeb release carried the headline [Riemann Computing Releases 13B Parameter AI Model Demo, Aims at Disrupting Model Training Costs](https://www.prweb.com/releases/riemann-computing-releases-13b-parameter-ai-model-demo-aims-at-disrupting-model-training-costs-302916102.html), and a later release on Newsfile Corp used the title Riemann Computing Publishes Technical Account of 13.1-Billion-Parameter AI Model Development. Three facts anchor the account. First, the model is a prerelease and the company labels it stage six of its growth ladder. Second, the complete loadable model sits on the Hugging Face Model Hub under the OpenPeerAI organization. Third, the work grew an existing small model instead of training a new one, which is the cost-saving claim the company keeps returning to. No named Riemann spokesperson appears on the record in the material we reviewed. The fact sheet we worked from carries no direct quotation and no price. This article therefore paraphrases documents and does not quote individuals. When a number appears below, it comes from the model card, the technical account or the press releases. When a number is our own arithmetic, we say so. ## The Spec Sheet at a Glance The table below collects the configuration the company published. Open Source AI.content: UPDATED 16:27 EST / NOVEMBER 06 2026 ### Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks. The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation. Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps. Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work. Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours. The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets. Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly. The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa. Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs. Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. Open Source AI.content: [Infosecurity Magazine Home](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/) » [News](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/) » [ARTEX Offensive AI Tool Activity Far Exceeds Reported Campaigns, Censys Finds](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/artex-activity-exceeds-reported/) # ARTEX Offensive AI Tool Activity Far Exceeds Reported Campaigns, Censys Finds [News](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/) ## Written by ![Photo of Kevin Poireault](https://assets.infosecurity-magazine.com/s3/infosec-media/images/profile/a7d280e2-8cd7-47a1-ba33-0ae2a304849f.png?width=64&height=64&mode=crop&scale=both&format=webp) ### [Kevin Poireault](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/profile/kevin-poireault/) Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine * [Follow @Kpoireault](http://twitter.com/Kpoireault) * [Connect on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevin-poireault-325ab283/) The use of a new AI-powered offensive security tool by cyber threat actors appears to be spreading well beyond the campaigns first identified. This tool, called ARTEX, is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘[Autumn-27](https://github.com/AUTUMN-27)’ in July 2026. While ARTEX has already been integrated in several known malicious campaigns since October, a new report by internet traffic scan provider Censys estimated its use could be much more widespread than previously thought. ## **ARTEX's Growing Use by Cyber Threat Actors** Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs). In October, two threat intelligence companies attributed its use as part of threat actor operations. First, in early October, CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to [a campaign against South Korean financial institutions](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-ai-korean-banks/). The analysts found ARTEX was used alongside Anthropic’s [Claude AI model](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/anthropic-claude-security-for-ai/) during the campaign, which ran from late September to early October 2026. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the attacker is a Chinese speaker and financially motivated. Microsoft attributed the campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned cyber threat actor also known as CovertNetwork-1658 or ORB07. The author claimed they were not involved in the ARTEX-linked attacks and that the tool was only meant for authorized penetration testing. Nevertheless, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO. In [a separate report](https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/inside-artex-how-autonomous-ai-agents-are-being-used-in-real-world-cyberattacks/), Check Point researchers showed AI agents in ARTEX control panels are running large-scale attacks with little human input for just a few hundred dollars, though they still fail and hallucinate successes. ## **Censys Uncover...

Infra & Chips.content: TAIPEI, Nov 6 (Reuters) - A global race to build AI infrastructure is unleashing billions of dollars of investment in advanced chip packaging, a once unglamorous aspect of technology that has become a critical bottleneck in turning out the world's most powerful processors. As demand for artificial intelligence chips outstrips available packaging capacity, companies from ​Nvidia (NVDA.O) and AMD (AMD.O) to lesser-known players in Taiwan are expanding production, while equipment makers develop new tools, interviews with more than a dozen industry executives and analysts show. "Packaging was always that thing that ‌you just didn't worry about," former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger, now a partner at Playground Global, told reporters in Taipei recently. Advanced packaging could eventually account for as much as half the value of a chip product, Gelsinger estimated, as some of today's graphics and central processing units can integrate 10 or more chips, sometimes as many as 20. Revenue from advanced packaging is forecast to overtake that earned via the traditional route for the first time in 2026, says research firm Yole Group, with capital spending on the technology expected to near $28 ​billion. ## TAIWAN FIRM DOMINATES CHIP-ON-WAFER SUBSTRATE The world's largest contract chipmaker, Taiwan's TSMC (2330.TW), dominates the most sophisticated advanced packaging technology, including chip-on-wafer-on-substrate, or CoWoS. The technology links separate pieces of silicon, such as processors and memory chips, on a shared ​base, to let them work together at high speed. It is widely used by Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom (AVGO.O), as well as cloud companies developing their own AI chips. But TSMC's capacity ⁠limits have spurred some chip designers to seek additional supply. Nvidia, for example, is providing billions of dollars in financing to expand CoWoS packaging capacity at Siliconware Precision Industries, or SPIL, a unit of Taiwan's ASE Technology (3711.TW), said an industry ​executive familiar with the matter, who sought anonymity for lack of authorisation to talk to media. The funding will support new factory space and equipment, the executive said. The scale of the support has not previously been reported. Nvidia did not respond ​to a request for comment. That allows the ensemble to work together faster as one system, in contrast with the practice of decades, when packaging served mainly to protect chips and provide the electrical connections to attach them to circuit boards. The shift comes as it ​become harder and costlier to win performance gains by shrinking and adding transistors, the tiny switches inside a chip. The newer packaging technique is especially important for AI chips, which need to shuffle vast amounts of data between processors and ​nearby memory. Speeding up such transfers hastens the process of training and running AI models. ## A RACE FOR TSMC ALTERNATIVES TSMC's tight capacity offers an opportunity for smaller suppliers, such as Taiwan's Powertech Technology (6239.TW). "Everyone is looking for a solution outside TSMC," its chairman, D K ‌Tsai, told reporters ⁠in August. "They don't want to rely entirely on TSMC." Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).AI-generated image Listen to this article6 min listen 00:0006:00 The AI infrastructure boom faces a critical stress test this week as [CoreWeave](https://www.coreweave.com) and [Nebius](https://nebius.com) prepare to report earnings against a backdrop of mounting inflation concerns that could reshape the Federal Reserve's interest rate strategy. The dual pressure of quarterly performance scrutiny and macro uncertainty arrives as AI data center stocks navigate growing voter backlash and capital intensity questions that have already rattled the sector. Wall Street's turning its attention to a pair of earnings reports that could either validate or undermine the massive bet investors have made on AI infrastructure. [CoreWeave](https://www.coreweave.com), the GPU cloud provider that's become a darling of the AI buildout, and [Nebius](https://nebius.com), the data center operator spun out of Yandex, are set to reveal whether the torrid demand for AI compute capacity translates into the kind of financial performance that justifies their sky-high valuations. The timing couldn't be more fraught. These earnings land just as a wave of inflation data threatens to upend the Fed's carefully calibrated rate policy. If the numbers run hot, the central bank may have to pump the brakes on rate cuts that AI infrastructure companies were counting on to finance their capital-intensive expansion plans. Higher-for-longer rates would hit these companies particularly hard given the billions they're pouring into GPU clusters and data center construction. Advertisement [CoreWeave](https://www.coreweave.com) has emerged as one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI arms race, providing the specialized infrastructure that companies like [OpenAI](https://openai.com) and [Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com) need to train and run their large language models. But the company's rapid expansion has raised questions about whether it can maintain margins while scaling at breakneck speed. Investors will be scrutinizing revenue growth, capacity utilization rates, and most critically, the company's ability to lock in long-term contracts that provide visibility into future cash flows. The broader context isn't helping. [Voter backlash against data centers erupted during the 2026 midterms](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/voters-block-data-centers-in-2026-midterms-across-ai-hotspots), with communities across AI hotspots rejecting new buildouts over concerns about power consumption, noise, and environmental impact. That grassroots revolt has already complicated expansion plans for the industry, and it's forcing companies to navigate an increasingly hostile regulatory landscape.
